text.transcript: What is RAG?
text.answer_preview: RAG means retrieve, then generate. The model does not answer from memory. We search our documents first, then we give those pieces to the model. I used this for BTEC exam questions so the output stays on the unit content.

text.transcript: What is agentic AI?
text.answer_preview: A chatbot replies in text. An agent is when the model chooses the next tool toward a goal, sees the result, and continues. My code runs the tool after checks. The model never gets a raw database because the prompt mentioned one.

text.transcript: What are guardrails in AI systems?
text.answer_preview: Guardrails are the checks around the model, before and after it. Before: validate input, catch injection, strip personal data, limit scope. text.transcript: What are embeddings?
text.answer_preview: An embedding is a long list of numbers that stands for a piece of text. An embedding model places similar meanings close together. Invoice and receipt sit near each other; invoice and car sit far. That is how semantic search and my assignment similarity checker work.

text.transcript: Can you explain how you used retrieval in your Ministry project?
text.answer_preview: Yes, at the Ministry, in question generation. I retrieve BTEC unit content and learning outcomes, then the model writes only from that text. JSON is checked, then a teacher approves. The similarity checker uses embeddings too, but it does not generate, so I do not call it RAG.

text.transcript: Tell me how retrieval helped your BTEC system
text.answer_preview: Because the source of truth is the unit file, and it changes. RAG lets me add or update a unit without retraining. Fine-tuning would bake old content into weights and still would not cite the page. Teachers needed to see that the question came from the outcome text. RAG plus a sc

text.transcript: Please walk me through the full path in your BTEC system from the source document through chunking embeddings retrieval generation validation and teacher approval.
text.answer_preview: I treat it as a pipeline test. If the gold chunk is not in the index, it is ingest or chunking. If it is in the index but not in top-k, it is embedding, filters, or query wording. If it is in the prompt and the model still fails, it is the prompt or the model, not retrieval.

text.transcript: If the retrieved context is wrong, what would you do?
text.answer_preview: The model will often still write a fluent answer, which is the danger. I try to prevent it: metadata filters, hybrid search for codes, re-rank, and a minimum similarity. text.transcript: Why does recall matter for the early warning model used by teachers?
text.answer_preview: Recall on the students who needed support. Most students were fine, so Accuracy looks high even if you miss the ones who matter. Missing a struggling student is worse than one extra follow-up. I still watched Precision so the list did not flood teachers.

text.transcript: What is RAG, how did you use it, and why did you choose it?
text.answer_preview: RAG means retrieve, then generate. I split documents into chunks, embed them, and store them with metadata.

text.transcript: Explain the assignment similarity checker, why it is not RAG, and who decides at the end.
text.answer_preview: LLM no, and RAG no, because nothing is generated. No, it is vector search and comparison: embeddings, similarity, and metadata filters. Students can copy and change the words, so exact matching misses that.

text.transcript: RAG architecture, risks, and business value.
text.answer_preview: I split documents into chunks, embed them, and store them with metadata. At question time I filter by access, search the nearest chunks, and pass that text to the model. I tell it to answer only from that text. Then I check the answer against the source.

text.transcript: Where do you store vectors in chroma DB?
text.answer_preview: Chroma is an open-source embedding store. A collection holds an id, a vector, the original text, and metadata. At query time I take nearest neighbors, optionally with a where filter. I used it in-process for prototypes. I have not run it as ministry production storage.

text.transcript: How does cosine similarity work with your embeddings?
text.answer_preview: Cosine similarity is the angle between two vectors, from minus one to one. Closer to one means closer meaning. Semantic search embeds the question, then finds stored chunks with nearby vectors. It can match supplier dues to paying creditors with almost no shared words.

text.transcript: Did you use scikit learn in the early warning model?
text.answer_preview: Python, Pandas, and sklearn: Pandas to clean and merge grades and attendance, sklearn for a pipeline with scaling and a classifier. I started with a simple model people could explain. I did not use a neural net, and I did not use an LLM or RAG.
